messages.body_plain:
On 11/7/11 4:52 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
 > The email was about the bugs rats example, which I checked in (what I
 > think is) a working version of. JAGS kills us on speed, but that's
 > only because it's a really easy problem and JAGS can therefore get
 > nearly independent samples every iteration.

I always say that benchmarking isn't easy to
make "objective".

I was expecting this sort of speed lag for simple
examples.  In fact, I brought it up with Andrew when he
was asking about BUGS/JAGS vs. Stan comparisons and with
Matt when we were talking about Stan vs. RM-HMC.

We should look better on scalability in terms of
amount of data, complexity and size of parameters,
and number of samples.  Judging from the lag at
the end of sampling, I think JAGS (like BUGS) buffers all
the samples in memory, but then maybe that's just an
R interface issue (which we'll probably inherit because
R's not scalable).

What I'd like to see is intrinsic model complexity on
the horizontal axis (e.g., number of predictors, data
size, etc.) versus resource usage on the vertical axis
(e.g., time or memory to get to a given ESS), with
lines for JAGS, NUTS (straight C++ implementation and
auto-dif implementation) and RM-HMC.

I think we'll look better than JAGS on more complex models
and at larger scale.  And we should look better than
RM-HMC at larger-scale models.

If it's only a compile time lag, we could work on that.

If it's something deeper, I also wrote into the proposal
that we'd build Gibbs with compilation.  That should run
faster than BUGS or JAGS (less compilation time).

> I just tried to write an email to stan-dev and was told I don't have
> permission. Could someone look into that?

Daniel's working on it.  I hope you're at least getting these
e-mails.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: return value for distributions outside of support?
messages.body_plain:
Daniel's working on error propagation for the
libs and we're now wondering what to do for
distributions given arguments outside their
support?

Sensible options seem to be either to

1.  return 0 (or -infinity on the log scale), or

2.  throw an exception

If we throw an exception, we'll probably want to make
it a special one so that someone could catch it
and go on, for instance by rejecting a sample.

Some of the more serious libs, like Boost, allow
you to configure error handling at a global level to
do one or the other, but I'd rather just go with one
for simplicity.

As Daniel brought up, in our case, it's almost
always going to be the result of either (a) some
arithmetic precision error, or (b) a model
specification error.  We can try to control (a) by
the same trick Matt applied to log1p(), namely
bounding returns in the expected range.

- Bob

Code generation would definitely make things faster (and much more
memory efficient, I think). It's tricky in general, but I suspect not
as hard for the average-case Stan model, which will usually just be a
sum of predefined functions of (possibly transformed) model variables.
Something to think about, especially because the memory cost of taping
poses real limitations on model size.

In this example, there's a surprising amount of overhead associated
with repeatedly computing log(sigma). It's not huge, and it'd probably
be a pain to eliminate, but we should add that sort of thing to the
list of sources of suboptimal efficiency.

BTW, on os x the "Time Profiler" in the Instruments application is a
really nice profiler. I think it's meant to replace Shark, which is
what I used to use. That's how I got alerted to the log(sigma)
business.

By "Gibbs is scale-invariant," I meant in the case where you've got
analytic conditionals for everything. It's a little less
scale-invariant when slice sampling using the doubling method, and
much less if you're using the stepping-out method. RMHMC does address
the issue of different parameters having different scales, but it goes
much further and (effectively) rotates the space so that the
parameters are locally uncorrelated. If you're dealing with a
multivariate normal target distribution, it basically tries to turn it
into a standard isotropic normal.

I think most distributions have sort of well defined behavior for
extreme parameter values—normals turn into deltas or improper uniforms
as sigma goes to 0 or inf, t's turn into normals or deltas as nu goes
to inf or 0, gammas turn into deltas as shape goes to 0 or rate goes
to inf, etc. IEEE math won't necessarily make these things happen like
they should by default. There's a little bit of a performance hit for
enforcing correct behavior, but it's probably pretty minor in c++
compared with evaluating logs and exps.

Matt

messages.subject: checking params & IEEE arithmetic
messages.body_plain:
I was just adding a vectorized normal_log and
looked at what Daniel's been up to adding
error conditions.  This is all on the right
track including the doc and error messages.

Unfortunately, we're going to need to change
the tests themselves, because IEEE isn't going
to do what you want in some of these cases.

The big problem is NaN, but the Inf cases can also be
problematic.

In particular, the condition under which we
want to raise an exception for a non-positive
scale parameter should be:

    !(sigma > 0)

which, unlike for real numbers (or even computer
represented int) is NOT the same condition as:

    sigma <= 0

If sigma is NaN, then (sigma <= 0) will fail, whereas
!(sigma > 0) will succeed.  And we definitely want
to trap NaN errors.

In general, any built-in function or operator applied
to NaN will return NaN.

Any test with a NaN component will fail (except in
short-circuit boolean operators):

0.0 * NaN  ==  NaN * 0  ==  NaN

(1 < NaN) == (1 > NaN) == (NaN > NaN) == false

((1 < 2) || (1 < NaN)) == true  [short circuit]
((1 > 2) && (1 < NaN)) == false [short circuit]

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Damn.  Not as much potential for vectorization
as I was recalling on the train.  But I did
replace the (sigma * sigma) with square(sigma)
and (x - mu) * (x - mu) with square(x-mu) in
the definition of the normal_log functions.

What I have now for the normal samples is:

data
   double y[N,T];

params
   double alpha[N];
   double beta[N];

BEFORE:

   for (n in 1:N) {
     alpha[n] ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
     beta[n] ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);
     for (t in 1:T)
       y[n,t] ~ normal(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar), sigma_y);
   }

AFTER:

   alpha ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha); // vectorized
   beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);  // vectorized
   for (n in 1:N)
     for (t in 1:T)
       y[n,t] ~ normal(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar), sigma_y);

I couldn't vectorize the y[n,t], because there's a varying
slope and varying intercept, so the gains from vectorization
here are going to be modest (they reduce the N logarithm
calcs and auto-difs in the alpha[n] and beta[n] samples to one).
But the squares do make some headway because they reduce the
size of memory and the number of allocations and stack ops we
need for auto-dif.

Profiling, the time's almost all taken in computing logs and in
pushing auto-dif variables onto and off of the stack.

I'm also seeing a huge amount of variance run to run,
which Matt thinks may have to do with the auto-tuning.
I'm getting everything from 3.5s to 15s in a set of
about ten runs.  So that'd leave JAGS 15-times to 75-times
faster for this example.

Needless to say, Matt's going to look into the root causes
of the variation.  We need to find the right answers and figure
out if we're at least getting those despite the time variations.
Ideally, we'll be able to reduce the inter-run variation in
time taken.  Intuitively, if the optimization gives you different
results, NUTS may need to run the leapfrog integrator for differing
number of steps.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: arithmetic errors with policy a la Boost
messages.body_plain:
Eureka!

Having just read the Boost math lib approach to
errors, I think we'd be well served to follow their
very sensible lead:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_47_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/main_overview/error_handling.html

The basic ideas are:

* a taxonomy of different kinds of errors (domain error,
   overflow, rounding, pole, etc.)

* four different actions on error (set error number,
   throw exception, ignore, user-defined)

* each pair of error-type and behavior results determines
   an action and return value

* final template parameter for error-handling policy that's
   set to a statically determined default controllable by macro

It'll also have two nice properties:  (a) our error handling
will be compatible with Boost's, and (b) we'll inherit the
documentation.

Along with this, we'll want to follow C++'s arithmetic and
the std lib's lead in returning NaN values where appropriate.
In most cases, we'll get this behavior for free propagated
through our results.  For instance, if we have a negative
variance and take its square root, we'll get a NaN which will
propagate to the result.

This is all based on the policy pattern, which is also used in Eigen
for arithmetic (it's what we're overriding to allow auto-dif
variables to integrate into Eigen).

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_47_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/policy/pol_overview.html

We already discussed using a template parameter with a default.

We're already using Boost's metaprogramming templates for
result type calculations:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_47_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/main_overview/result_type.html

so we're already compatible there.

The one issue I didn't see the answer to is whether to check
all arguments, even if some are unused.  This'll come up when
we override the log probability functions to only compute
up to a proportion.  Some constants aren't actually used, but
may be out of range.

It's a lot of work to do all this the right way, but I
think it'll turn out to be easier in the long run in terms
of saving on doc and consistency and compatibility.  On that
note, I leave you with:

http://xkcd.com/974/

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I checked in a new file stan/prob/ag_distributions.hpp, which
specializes normal_log() to do the autodiff gradient calculations more
efficiently. Whereas before calling normal_log() would do autodiff
through all of the calculations needed to compute the normal log
probability, the new specialized version computes the gradients
analytically, which turns out to be a good amount faster, like a
factor of 2 over the previous version on the rats example. This is
comparable to the speed I get when doing "by hand" code generation
using adjoint variables, and within a factor of two of the speed I get
with more highly tuned handwritten gradient code. All of which seems
to suggest that this is something that we should be doing for other
distributions too.

I've also checked in a version of rats.cpp* that illustrates how to
use the new ag_distributions implementation. You can test the speed
change on your own machine by commenting out "#include
<stan/prob/ag_distributions.hpp>".

We should probably think harder about what the right way to do these
implementations is in general—I just threw something together quickly
as a proof of concept.

Matt

*This model expresses things in terms of precisions instead of
deviations, but the differences should be minimal.

That's great.  I figured we'd start doing these

faster.

We should eventually do all the distributions.  With
design as it stands, we should be able to drop

backward compatible.  We can keep going with
structured subroutines for reusable parts of models.
I've been planning out the within-Stan subroutine
language, but that won't make things go faster.

The matrix ops could use the same treatment -- many
of them have easy analytical derivatives.  Including
Ben's covariance encoding. It's just an awful lot of code
and doc to deal with.  Daniel and I did just get error
handling sorted and this is another argument for doing
things with the kind of helper functions he set up.

The next step is to get rid of constant terms from
the calc.  We can do that with template overrides.
For example, what we have now is:

   template <typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_scale>
   calculated_type
   normal_log(T_y y, T_loc mu, T_scale sigma);

What we eventually need is eight template overrides based on
whether T_y, T_loc, T_scale are stan::agrad::var
or double instances.  Then for each instance, drop all
the terms that just involve double values as they'll be
in the constant normalizer.  For instance,
we can use the following for non-hierarchical regression
priors:

   template <>
   var
   normal_log(var y, double mu, double sigma) {
       ... doesn't involve log(sigma) term ...
   }

Then we can drop any terms in the sum that only have
double args as they're just constant normalizing terms.

Then we can do the same thing with multiple  samples,
adding another 8 versions with std::vector<T_y>
as the first arg in the general case.
For the normal, that saves a whole lot of log calcs
if the scale is stan::agrad::var.

For consistency, the code should go in namespace
stan::agrad and in file stan/agrad/distributions.hpp.  This
will require more includes, though I want to
add some higher-level includes like all the other
packages use.

- Bob

>
> I'm trying to figure out how the hell Boost does their stuff. I trust

Whatever's easiest.  Boost breaks out their functions and
then provides higher-level includes that reference the files.

> Regarding their stuff, have you seen something like this before?
 >
> template<class T, class Policy>
> inline typename tools::promote_args<T>::type erf(T z, const Policy&  /* pol */)
>
> I can't figure out what's going on with the "const Policy&" without a
> variable declaration. I don't even know how to search for that. The
> rest of it seems straightforward (enough).

No, but I looked at the example in boost/math/special_functions/erf.cpp
and I think I see what's going to happen in practice.
The key is that even though the actual value will
be ignored, its type won't be.  So if we have:

   double y;
   SomePolicyImpl p;
   double v = erf(y,p);

then type inference will ensure that the actual instance
that gets called is erf<double,SomePolicyImpl>.  That will
ensure SomePolicyImpl gets used appropriately in the template
metaprogramming for the implementation, including for error
handling throughout.  Note that the template parameter
Policy is used throughout the body of the definition of erf().

W/o the argument, the call would've had to have been:

double v = erf<double,SomePolicyImpl>(y);

because the policy is the second template argument.

They also include the template override with the
default policy:

template <class T>
inline typename tools::promote_args<T>::type erf(T z)
{
    return boost::math::erf(z, policies::policy<>());
}

So you can also use erf with the default by just
calling erf(y).

messages.subject: rats comparisons
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I tried running Metropolis on the rats example using various rescaled proposal distributions. The results are:
1. It takes forever to burn in without rescaling. Longer than I was willing to wait (20 minutes).
2. If you initialize it at the posterior mean and use an isotropic Gaussian proposal distribution (scaled to get near .234 accept rate) you get a minimum ESS of about 40 after 1M iterations.
3. If you initialize it at the posterior mean and use a Gaussian proposal distribution with diagonal covariance equal to the variance of the posterior (scaled to get near .234 accept rate), you get a minimum ESS of about 24 after 10K iterations, which is about 60x better than unscaled.
4. If you initialize it at the posterior mean and use a Gaussian proposal distribution with full covariance equal to the covariance of the posterior (scaled to get near .234 accept rate), you get a minimum ESS of about 20 after 10K iterations, which is indistinguishable from diagonal covariance.

By contrast:
5. NUTS with no rescaling and good initialization gets a minimum ESS of about 500 using about 100K gradient evaluations, which is around 2x as efficient as Metropolis with good scaling.
6. NUTS with step size rescaling (equivalent to diagonal covariance for Metropolis) gets a minimum ESS of about 500 using about 7K gradient evaluations, which is about 30x as efficient as Metropolis with good scaling.
(These comparisons ignore the extra cost of gradient evaluations, which is sort of cheating.)

Finally:
7. JAGS gets about 3300 effective samples using 10K sweeps, which is about 4-5x as efficient as rescaled NUTS.
(This comparison ignores possible differences between the cost of gradient evaluations and the cost of Gibbs sweeps.)

So in summary, here's a Girolami and Calderhead style table:

Sampler                Normalized ESS
raw Metropolis         1
diagonal Metropolis    60
full-cov Metropolis    50
raw NUTS               125
rescaled NUTS          1785
JAGS                   8250

If we took away the model's conjugacy, JAGS would get hit by a pretty big penalty for reverting to slice sampling. I'd guess a factor of 10–20, which would make its performance worse than rescaled NUTS. So that's encouraging.

Matt

PS: This evaluation assumes we already know the covariance matrix of the target distribution, and discounts any additional cost involved in finding it during burn-in/inefficiencies before we've found it. Which is probably a big deal.

messages.body_plain:
It's a little surprising, I agree. It might have something to do with the Radfordian argument about random walks over the range of values of the log-posterior probability. For this model, the log-posterior probability (hereafter referred to as logp) has a range of about 25. In section 5.4.4 of Radford's HMC chapter, he argues that if you've got a target distribution whose variables are i.i.d., then Metropolis kernels that are tuned to a .234 acceptance rate should produce proposals whose changes in logp are approximately normally distributed with mean -2.8 and variance 5.6. If you simulate the resulting process (including rejections), then it can actually take hundreds of iterations to cover a range of 25.

But I'm not sure there isn't a flaw in my (interpretation of Radford's) reasoning. So I ran 10K Metropolis steps on a 65-dimensional (like the rats example) standard normal distribution with jumps tuned to get about .23 acceptance probability, and got a min ESS of about 25. Which is pretty damn close to 1/500. So it looks like that's about as good as it's possible for Metropolis to do for a target distribution with this dimensionality, since it doesn't get much easier than an isotropic normal. (Metropolis would do better in terms of ESS/sweep if you ran it on each dimension independently for this example. But maybe not in terms of ESS/function evaluation.)

Matt

It's not that you aren't moving at all, it's that you aren't moving in specific dimensions. If you're underestimating the appropriate scale for some dimension at 1/1000th of what it should be, then you'll make progress in all of the other dimensions but not in that one. So basically you're doing anti-Gibbs. Tuning acceptance rates works as usual, because you still need to reject moves in the other dimensions. I've been tuning the sum of the scales, not the determinant—it could be that the determinant (or geometric mean for diagonal scaling) is a better choice. But regardless of how we measure overall scale this problem can still come up if we do a really bad job of estimating relative scales initially, e.g., because we're using samples along the trajectory from the initial state to the target high-mass region to estimate standard deviations.

messages.subject_clean: Stan vs. JAGS, NUTS vs. Gibbs, etc.
messages.body_plain:
1.  There are two levels to this evaluation:

a.  Gibbs vs. NUTS

b.  JAGS vs. Stan

If Gibbs and NUTS have the same complexity, then it
comes down to implementation.  If we consider things
like parallelization part of implementation, there
are tradeoffs between Gibbs and NUTS/HMC in that the
former can block parallelize in some cases whereas
NUTS/HMC can parallelize gradient calcs.

2.  There are different kinds of scaling issues:

a.  number of data items

b.  number of parameters

c.  number of samples we want

Relative performance will vary.  (2c) is especially
important in that NUTS involves a tuning step and
Stan involves a compilation step.  Compilation and tuning
both involve up-front costs that are then amortized based
on the number of samples we want.

This is in addition to the scaling in terms of model
complexity, which is itself hard to measure.

3.  On that note, there are two things we care about:

a.  speed (i.e., wall clock time)

b.  space (i.e., memory)

JAGS and Stan have different behaviors here.  We'll do real
well scaling on data size in terms of space.  If there aren't
involved iterative matrix calcs, we'll also win on parameter
scaling in terms of space.

4.  How much tuning do we allow?  That is, there are implementation
details within JAGS or Stan that matter.  For instance, in
Stan, we can write directly in C++ or use the graphical-model
compiler.  If we go with C++, we can use auto-dif or hand-code
our derivatives.  If we hand-code derivatives, there are further
optimizations based on whether we use a brute-force adjoint
method or get more clever with intermediate calculations and
sufficient stats.  The same holds for JAGS in terms of using
redundant parameters, etc.

- Bob

We're only talking about continuous parameters for now.

I'm pretty sure that R2WinBUGS and R2jags calculate
R-hat using the positive-only deviation (or variance or
precision) parameters, rather than applying a log transform.
R2jags even treats a 5-way categorical variable as a
continuous variable in [1,5] instead of using a 4-way (or
5-way) binary encoding.  (The other problem with monitoring
discrete parameters for mixtures is that often 1000 samples
all put a point in the same mixture component and therefore
get an effective sample size of 1.)

This is going to be a huge amount of work if we have to
transform all the JAGS models' outputs.   Although we have the
transform code, we don't have the variable typings we
need to synch the transforms with JAGS's output.  I'm not
even sure how we could do that in general without writing
another language for specifying it and parsing it or just
writing one-off code for each model, either of which is likely
to be error prone (as is our recoding, but we test our output
vs. that reported in BUGS).

The transforms are trivial for deviation and binomial
parameters, but much less so for ordered logit cutpoints,
multinomial parameters and covariance matrices.

Thanks.  I'm cc-ing the entire development team (Andrew Gelman
ended up naming the project Stan after Stanislaw Ulam -- it's not
an acronym).

 > in your implementations for similar things do you have ways to
 > auto-tune
 > the parameters (mass matrix etc)? or have you considered reimannian
 > manifold HMC? parameter tuning is definitely a flaw in the
 > automactiness
 > of our implementation...

Matt Hoffman has a very nice solution to the tuning
problem for both step size and number of steps.
Here's a link to the writeup:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4246

Matt's been looking into non-identity and I think even
some non-diagonal mass matrix issues lately to see if
we can get more speedups that way, perhaps with a low-rank
approximation for large numbers of dimensions (we want
to be able to run hierarchical regressions with at least thousands
of predictors).

 > anyhow, i'll be curious to hear what you all are up to.

We're pretty far along at this point -- about to release
the first version.

One of the bigger problems was transforming variables
so there weren't any hard boundaries
(the alternative is to bounce).  We deal with bounded
below, bounded above, bounded below and above, simplexes,
ordered positive numbers, correlation matrices and
covariance matrices.  The last two are particularly
tricky -- Ben Goodrich implemented a Cholesky-decomposition
version of the Lewandowski et al. C-vine transform.
This then plays into specifying the data, the
initial values, and getting output out.

We've also been playing with coding various kinds of
models involving missing data, ordered logit, bounded
normals where the bounds are parameters, and that kind
of thing, all of which are challenging on the transform
front.

We're still evaluating on more test cases.  Right now,
we're implementing all the BUGS example models.

- Bob

messages.subject: stan::agrad::var numeric limits and operator<<
messages.body_plain:
I added a template override for

     std::numeric_limits<stan::agrad::var>

at the end of stan/agrad/agrad.hpp.   Here's
some general doc on numeric_limits:

     http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/std/limits/numeric_limits/

I just have it return the same values as std::numeric_limits<double>.
Most of the return vals are primitives, but some return instances of
stan::agrad::var.  For example, I define quiet_NaN, which is
what Boost error checking returns for NaN values under some
error policies, as follows:

   static stan::agrad::var quiet_NaN() {
     return numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
   }

The potential problem is that this will create a new stan::agrad::var
on the auto-dif stack every time it's called.
So I'm hoping it only happens when there's an error.  I
think this'll be ok for quiet_NaN, but I'm not so
sure about min() and other things.

The default non-specialized implementation just throws
exceptions for all these things that would otherwise
return instances, so if we're not throwing those exceptions
now, we're probably OK going forward with real values.

I had to do similar overrides of numerical
traits in the Eigen namespace so it could figure out what
to do with auto-dif variables in matrix ops.

I also modified the operator<< for streaming output to
produce both the value and adjoint value.  I also
documented it.

- Bob
